items.title: Hamilton leads final practice after Leclerc lap deletion
items.author: Matt Beer
items.content:
Ferrari completed a full set of top United States Grand Prix Formula 1 practice times in the final session at Austin, though a track limits deletion for Charles Leclerc meant this time it was Lewis Hamilton on top.

Friday pacesetter Leclerc lost a time that had been 0.083 seconds faster than Hamilton, falling to third behind Max Verstappen as a result as he had to rely on a medium-tyre time.

Ferrari had also been on top during the longer runs in the first part of the session before teams switched to qualifying simulations.

Hamilton expressed his frustration with Gabriel Bortoleto over a traffic incident - one of quite a few in the session - that will be looked at by the stewards.

Leclerc was far from the only driver to fall foul of track limits as the wild number of laptime deletions continued through the session. Championship leader Kimi Antonelli and both McLaren drivers were among the other high-profile transgressors.

Though Leclerc's lap loss meant Red Bull ended the session second with Verstappen, both he and Isack Hadjar had plenty of complaints over team radio and Verstappen having a wild lock-up, slide and wheelspin moment to end his session.

Alex Albon also received Hadjar's team radio ire - albeit for an 'impeding' incident that looked like it only happened because a big mistake from Hadjar carried him towards the slower-moving Williams.

Antonelli ended up fourth ahead of Mercedes team-mate George Russell.

The laptime deletions helped Nico Hulkenberg to get Audi as high as seventh, splitting the McLarens.

items.title: Herta could replace Bottas at Cadillac in F1 2027
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Cadillac's 2027 Formula 1 driver line-up isn't yet finalised, with reserve driver Colton Herta among those in contention to replace Valtteri Bottas.

Both Bottas and Sergio Perez joined F1's 2026 new team Cadillac on long-term deals, but The Race understands the team hasn't made a final decision on who will drive for it next year.

In the Austin press conference on Friday, Cadillac team boss Marcin Budkowski left the door open when asked if Perez and Bottas will stay on for 2027.

"This is the last place I would comment on driver contracts, and in general, I think it's not something that is done in the press," Budkowski said.

"It's something which will be done by official releases from the team when the time is right."

Cadillac has to decide between sticking with the continuity of its two experienced drivers with knowledge of championship-winning teams or whether it's the right time to make a change with potentially bigger upsides for the future.

There's nothing to suggest Perez is at risk of losing his seat, as he's been the stronger Cadillac driver this year and has pushed the team hard behind-the-scenes to improve.

Bottas and Perez have been fairly evenly matched in qualifying this year, with Perez leading Bottas 13-9, but it's in the races where Perez has had a clear margin. Bottas has only spent 18% of the racing laps they've both been on track ahead of Perez.

Bottas has also had some particularly tough grands prix, including the last race in Singapore, where he was lapping around 1.5 seconds slower than Perez without a clear explanation.

That means his seat is in doubt for 2027, with 26-year-old Herta among those who could replace him.

Why "disappointing" F2 season hasn't hurt Herta's chances 

Herta has had a self-described "disappointing" F2 campaign as he's 19th out of 22 full-time drivers with two rounds in Qatar and Abu Dhabi remaining.  

"Maybe a few more questions than answers for me, maybe more questions than going into it, so I'm fairly disappointed with everything on that side of things," Herta said at Austin. 

"I'm just disappointed with how the year's gone; it's not been good at all."

It's unlikely Herta will stay in F2 for a second season next year, but he's made it clear he'd still like a racing programme of some kind next year, with F1 still the ultimate goal.

Cadillac isn't put off by Herta's disappointing F2 performances as it knew making the switch would be difficult, and it's been impressed by the work Herta has done in its F1 car.

It does mean, however, that Herta's championship finish is all but certain not to earn him any superlicence points from F2, but Cadillac is ensuring he'll reach the 40-point threshold.

Herta took part in his fourth FP1 of the year at Austin on Friday, but only three of those are eligible for the superlicence bonus point, as a technical issue at Monza meant he didn't clear the 100km of running necessary to gain the superlicence point.

That, added together with his IndyCar results - including 30 points for finishing runner-up to champion Alex Palou in 2024 - means he's now one point away from the threshold.

The Race understands Herta will do another FP1 before the end of the year to make sure he gets to 40 points so he can be an option for 2027.

Herta has also completed private F1 testing away from the circuit, having run in an Alpine as part of that team's Testing of Previous Cars programme at Portimao, where he ran in a ground effect-era car.

Cadillac doesn't have a TPC programme of its own, so, just as when it ran Perez in an old Ferrari in late 2025, it's struck a deal with a rival team to ensure Herta gets more mileage.

Since first gunning for an F1 entry under the Andretti banner, Cadillac has long stated its ambition to have an American driver if one can earn a seat on merit with Herta the most logical candidate.

Herta isn't the only contender for Bottas's seat, as multiple drivers have been contacting Cadillac - it's the only ‘open' seat, with Racing Bulls only picking between Red Bull-contracted drivers. 

Esteban Ocon is looking for a way to stay on the F1 grid next year after losing his seat to Ferrari junior Rafael Camara, but The Race understands he won't be joining Cadillac in a race or reserve driver role.

Instead, he's likely to take a reserve driver role at a different team such as Aston Martin.

Red Bull reserve driver Yuki Tsunoda is looking for a permanent return to the grid after his unexpected three-race return with Racing Bulls earlier this year.

Tsunoda's representatives have been contacting Cadillac over a 2027 opportunity and he is among the contenders.

Cadillac isn't in a rush to make a final decision, as none of the candidates have race seat options elsewhere.

Should it elect to replace Bottas for 2027, it would need to come to some kind of arrangement given he has a long-term deal with the team.

items.title: Ferrari's last major 2026 F1 upgrade explained
items.author: Gary Anderson
items.content:
Ferrari has arrived in Austin with what should be its last Formula 1 car update of 2026.

From what we can see, it’s not a massive change - just small changes to the details in various areas, but as I often say, they all add up.

To be honest, Ferrari has not been that far behind as far as performance is concerned. It's been points lost through execution and decision-making. I know that Lewis Hamilton put his hand up as to not pitting under the VSC in Singapore, for instance, but that’s just one example of Ferrari's indecisions costing it.

Without doubt, Hamilton has lots of experience when it comes to making pit calls - some good, some bad - but my concern with the driver overruling the team is that for any driver, they only have their own information, and at most that of the cars in front and behind them, as to what the tyre situation is. The team has - or at least should have - the information from all of the cars still running, so a much broader picture of what is happening, so it should be able to make a better decision.

I say 'should' here because I have no idea if Ferrari looks any further than its own cars and also there seems to be a bit of a reluctance for anyone to put their heads above the parapet. If you don’t make decisions, you can never be held responsible for making the wrong decision.

Ferrari has also thrown away quite a few points by not allowing whatever driver is fastest to just press on - again, that falls into the reactiveness of decision making.

Anyway, that’s my moan for today - onto the developments. As I said, from what I can see, it is small detail changes.

The purple fin separating the radiator intake from the coke bottle undercut seems to have increased in size slightly. As the car speed increases, the radiator will not be able to flow the volume of air that is presented to it - when this happens, the inlet duct will start to spill around the outer body surface. This fin will reduce the adverse effect this spillage would have on the undercut sidepod.

In reality, it means that the floor foot vanes (bargeboards) will perform more consistently.

As for the sidepods, there's a change to the overall profile. The upper surface is now lower at the rear, inducing more downwash over that upper surface. This means that the sidepod's volume at its trailing edge has been reduced, opening up the coke bottle section between the inside of the rear brake duct and the inner body surface.

Also, the small undercut below the CEVA decal looks like it has also been increased in depth. These small changes in body profile reduce the amount of airflow that is presented to the outer edge of the underfloor - airflow in that area will be pulled under the underfloor by the low pressure underneath the car, and in turn that will reduce the overall downforce produced by the underfloor.

To go hand in hand with the changes at the sidepod inlet and the sidepod itself are novelties in the diffuser area. On the outer upper trailing edge corner, Ferrari has gone from a simple gurney flap (highlighted in green) to a more sophisticated vane (highlighted in purple). This outer corner is one area that can suffer from airflow separation problems. The new vane connects it to the multiple turning vanes mounted on the inner surface of the rear brake ducts.

Ferrari has also introduced changes to the diffuser vanes (highlighted in blue). There are probably further changes, but the obvious is the different trim to the lower trailing edge corner - this new detail should instigate a vortex, perhaps even two vortices, coming off that now-90° rear corner. If so, this will help seal that splitter to the track surface, improving the performance of the actual diffuser inboard of them.

Anything like this, when you are attempting to work the diffuser and underfloor harder, can very easily increase sensitivity to the track surface so lead to pointy downforce. However, in Austin, because of the bumpy track surface, Ferrari will probably be running the car just that little bit softer and, with that, a millimetre or two higher. The same is true for other teams that might be suffering from the same problems - so Mercedes might be able to get a better performance from its updates introduced in Malaysia (Bahrain).

Overall, it’s great to see at least four teams and eight drivers battling with each other, that’s what racing should be about - on top of that, as a small team, it is good to see Racing Bulls keeping those four big teams honest.

items.title: Gary Anderson's simple design solution for F1's impeding problem
items.author: Gary Anderson
items.content:
Every Formula 1 race weekend, there are constant complaints about drivers being blocked when on a fast lap. Expect more when United States Grand Prix qualifying happens later today.

Yet there is a simple solution that could be implemented immediately to prevent these near-misses.

The extent of the problem is obvious. There have been stewards’ investigations into impeding on 12 out of 17 race weekends already this year, with a total of 14 punishments issued, some of those grid penalties. And even when it doesn’t go this far, the airwaves are filled with drivers complaining about being held up over the radio.

This doesn’t need a complicated fix that requires you to reinvent the wheel or spend huge amounts of money. It doesn’t even need something new to be added.

Simply change the regulations to double the size of the rear-view mirrors and more closely define the ideal position for those.

By 'ideal' I don’t mean aerodynamically ideal - I mean for the driver’s line of sight.

To give an idea of the size, I’ve highlighted what I would do in white on the Mercedes in the image on the right. You can see the comparison to the current standard size mirrors on the Red Bull on the left.

Yes, it will create a little more drag and make the aero design more difficult, but it’s more important to reduce the number of times qualifying is changed by impeding.

Then the emphasis can be on the driver to be responsible for their actions. The mirror position will be specified - and to ensure that nobody attempts to exploit any grey areas or loopholes, you can have a supplementary test that requires a driver to be able to sit in the cockpit and read something on a board placed in specified positions behind the car. So like an eye test, but backwards.

We often hear about the drivers’ rear-view mirrors vibrating. Surely this problem is not beyond the might of F1 and its design teams to solve. And if it is, there are numerous vibration specialists out there that would be only too happy to come up with a solution.

If a team enters a car that still suffers mirror vibration problems, then that comes under 'dangerous construction'. If the driver can’t see a car behind them, then they have to suffer the consequences of the situation that the team has put them into.

There are occasions when the drivers have had penalties reduced or sometimes even dropped entirely because of poor information from the pitwall. Yes, it is helpful to have this information and it should continue - but the onus to comply should be on the driver.

By giving the drivers better visibility, it would give them no excuses for not paying attention.

items.title: Sports must ditch 'obsession' over F1's success
items.author: Samarth Kanal
items.content:
Formula 1’s success has triggered a wave of aspirants as other sports try to match the same meteoric rise in popularity that F1 has enjoyed under owner Liberty Media.

But are those other sports too focused on following F1’s footsteps over playing to their own strengths? 

That’s the hypothesis that Antonio Cacorino, CEO and founder of APEX, offered to Darren Cox and the audience at 'Formula One's Premium Playbook', an event hosted by The Race and Axios.

APEX is a sports-focused investment firm backed by more than 100 athletes including F1’s Lando Norris, Carlos Sainz, and Valtteri Bottas. It also owns a minority stake in the Alpine F1 team.

Cacorino said that F1’s growth is down to a “combination of different factors that all clicked together”, including the regularly cited effect of Netflix’s Drive to Survive reality series. 

“Timings were also quite important," he added. "People don't realise the fact that Drive to Survive Season 2 was being pushed by Netflix exactly when the whole world stopped and everyone was stuck at home in COVID [in early 2020]. That also helped.

“But in life, sometimes you also need certain things to click. And they understood that was in their favour. And then obviously the result is here.”

Drive to Survive spawned a documentary race since it premiered in 2019, with the likes of golf's PGA Tour (Full Swing), professional tennis (Break Point), road cycling (Tour de France: Unchained) and NASCAR (Full Speed) following suit. Yet how successful those series were at exposing those sports to new audiences has been hard to judge.

“We already see the amount of sports content that Netflix is putting out. Obviously, we're at the stage where there's too much content,” said Cacorino. 

“So, it's very hard to achieve the same success. Obviously, F1 did with Drive to Survive. But I do think it's that kind of content and that kind of media play is something that a lot of the big sports need to do.

“But only once you've achieved certain status. Other sports should maybe have those kinds of strategies, but maybe kind of as a way to bring a bit more eyeballs and then monetise through sponsorships or through other alternatives.

"I don't think that should be an obsession, because it's very hard to replicate. Now there's thousands of sports trying to do it.”

F1’s growth during and after the global pandemic, thanks to its unique position as one of the first sports to return to competition during that time, the Drive to Survive effect, and the 2021 championship fight between Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen, helped it become the juggernaut it is now. 

Asked on stage if he sees any risks on the horizon for F1, Cacorino said: “To be honest, I don't see many risks. I think it's too big to fail.

“It's reached, really, a level where fans are here to stay. I don't think there's any other sport challenging. 

“Obviously you can get regulatory changes, a new potential owner can come in and maybe take it in a different direction. But I do think that F1 has reached a position where it's here to stay. It's this global IP that brands will want to come in.

“Fans are always going to be here consuming the sport. There's always going to be more and more different drivers and stars coming up. 

“So I think there's few risks, just general macro[economic] risks that any other sector can take. 

“But I would say there's nothing structural that would call for a risk. Hence the long-term vision I have that I would invest today and stay as an investor for a long time.”

items.title: Fernandez becomes sixth rider sidelined from Australian GP
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
Defending Australian Grand Prix winner Raul Fernandez has been named as the sixth full-time MotoGP rider sidelined from this year’s Phillip Island race.

Fernandez joins Fermin Aldeguer (Gresini Ducati), Joan Mir (Honda), Luca Marini (Honda), Toprak Razgatlioglu (Pramac Yamaha) and Jorge Martin (Aprilia) as an absentee from Sunday’s event.

Aldeguer, Mir and Razgatlioglu are missing the weekend due to various injury and health reasons and an ill Marini had to throw in the towel after two laps in practice, while Martin got injured in the sprint.

Fernandez, meanwhile, is nursing an injury from Mandalika - where he had to use a different braking technique in the grand prix race after sustaining a right index finger fracture in the sprint start crash  - and was forced to drop out of the Australian GP sprint by his physical condition.

His Trackhouse team has now confirmed that his Phillip Island weekend is over, and that he is in doubt for next weekend's round at Sepang, which offers no shortage of braking challenges.

"After the race, Fernandez went straight to a medical assessment with the MotoGP medical director [Dr Angel Charte] and it was found that while the finger fracture is stable, there is inflammation of the soft tissue around the fracture," Trackhouse explained.

Fernandez will have a medical assessment on Thursday at Sepang so is at least set to attend the weekend.

His absence brings the grand prix field down to 18 bikes, as only two of the six absentees are being covered by stand-ins.

Gresini has Iker Lecuona on Aldeguer’s Ducati and Augusto Fernandez will complete the season on Razgatlioglu’s Pramac Yamaha.

But while Fernandez, Martin and Marini’s withdrawals all happened during Saturday, Honda was already unable to cover for Mir because its test riders Taka Nakagami and Aleix Espargaro are also injured. So Marini dropping out as well leaves its works team with no bikes on the grid.

items.title: Arm injury effectively ends Martin's MotoGP title chance
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
Jorge Martin and his Aprilia MotoGP team have suffered a huge blow in the 2026 title race, with at least one fracture discovered after his crash in the Phillip Island sprint.

Martin exited the sprint race at the fast Hayshed corner (Turn 8) after a multi-lap lead battle with title rival Marc Marquez.

He rolled violently through the gravel and was taken to the medical centre on a stretcher, before emerging from it with his right arm in a cast.

Aprilia subsequently revealed that Martin has fractured his right arm - and while he will still require further examinations to determine the full extent of the damage, he has been declared unfit for the remainder of the Phillip Island weekend.

According to Aprilia, a fracture to the right radial bone - one of the two primary bones in the forearm - has been definitively diagnosed. But there is also a suspected fracture to the other primary forearm bone, the ulna, "at the distal end" (which means towards the wrist rather than the elbow).

No recovery timeline has been outlined given the absence of a full diagnosis, but the injury makes it all but impossible for Martin to realistically remain in this title race.

He is 10 points behind Marquez in the standings and will miss Sunday's race, but the injury has also come at the start of a planned triple-header (covering also the Sepang race and the in-doubt Qatar race).

Martin had suffered two radial fractures already (both on the left arm) earlier in his grand prix career.

One came during the 2018 season in Moto3, forcing him to miss one race but with a quick enough recovery to enable him to win the title that year, while the other happened before the start of the 2025 season and (along with a spate of other injuries from the same crash) sidelined him for two rounds.

items.title: Marquez retakes MotoGP lead after epic duel and big Martin crash
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
Defending MotoGP champion Marc Marquez took a crucial victory in the sprint race at Phillip Island, as title rival Jorge Martin crashed out from their epic duel.

It was the dry sprint Aprilia would have hoped for given Marquez's supremacy in the wet in qualifying earlier today - but instead it suffered a heavy title blow, and Martin faces fitness concerns after being stretchered off from the site of his crash.

Martin had gone fourth-to-second at the start, though had to fight off a counter-attack from Alex Marquez during the second lap as a five-bike lead group established itself.

But as Martin challenged Marc Marquez out front, a lunge on Alex by Pedro Acosta allowed the lead duo breathing room - and they spent the next handful of laps in a back-and-forth squabble for the lead.

Martin would repeatedly take first and then give it up through errors - going wide at the Miller corner, then at the Southern Loop - or to Marc counter-attacks.

Finally, with Alex bearing down on them again after fighting off Acosta, it proved one counter-attack too many for Martin - who crashed at speed coming through Hayshed and rolled violently in the gravel.

He didn't immediately look in obvious strife in the aftermath of the crash, but then was put on a stretcher and taken to the medical centre for checks.

Marc Marquez controlled the race from there, with no real challenge forthcoming from Alex, and now heads Martin by 10 points in the standings.

Fabio Di Giannantonio (VR46 Ducati) and Marco Bezzecchi (Aprilia) worked their way through the order, having sat seventh and 10th after the start, and just ran out of laps to challenge for second place.

Bezzecchi now trails Marc Marquez by 50 points in the standings.

Acosta, Ai Ogura, Brad Binder, home hero Jack Miller and 'lone Honda standing' Diogo Moreira initially made up the points.

But Ogura faced an investigation for a potential tyre pressure infringement, and when his penalty was applied Gresini Ducati stand-in Iker Lecuona picked up a point.

Martin was the only rider to crash out - but there were four other retirements in Raul Fernandez (seemingly fitness-related), Maverick Vinales, Pecco Bagnaia and Johann Zarco, the latter bowing out due to an apparent mechanical issue while in the top five.

items.title: How F1's top four teams are comparing in Austin
items.author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
items.content:
Formula 1's United States Grand Prix looks poised to be a multi-team fight for victory based on how the top four teams have started at Austin.

Here are the early clues about the pecking order, with single-lap and long-run pace trends painting very different pictures.

The combination of the varying strengths of the leading cars and the wide range of corner speeds of the Austin circuit that tests every facet of a car means that Ferrari, Red Bull and Mercedes, which were separated by less than two tenths on single-lap pace, all excelled and struggled at different parts of the track.

Pacesetter Charles Leclerc was strongest in the slow corners. He carried the highest minimum speed at Turn 1, matched Kimi Antonelli's best at Turn 12, and braked late for the Turn 11 hairpin without compromising his exit. He was often first back on the throttle.

In the high-speed sections, Leclerc was quickest through Turns 6-7, keeping part-throttle where Max Verstappen lifted - however, at times the picture in the fast corners was muddied by deployment variations. As always, the Ferrari lost significant time on the straights - just over six tenths relative to Verstappen.

Verstappen's Red Bull was mighty on the straights, gaining around six tenths on Leclerc once the speeds had settled, and a little over a tenth compared to the Mercedes. That characteristic also gave him a strong start to the lap down the start/finish straight. He was committed on the brakes in terms of stopping power, but was often later on the throttle at slow-corner exits, with that approach paying off at Turn 20, where he had a strong exit.

Where Red Bull is lacking most for Verstappen was obvious after a pretty good day left the four-time F1 world champion seeking a finer balance rather than anything drastic.

"It's clearly the low-speed performance that we are focused on at the moment," was Red Bull technical director Pierre Wache's verdict when asked by The Race if there was a standout area to improve overnight.

"Low speed is the key for us."

That aforementioned Verstappen preference for braking slightly earlier, but harder, to prioritise a good exit was clear throughout the lap but, other than at Turn 20, it did not really manifest in laptime due to the Red Bull seemingly lacking rotation.

Verstappen's Turn 1 was the worst of the top three. Despite braking earliest he was slowest back to full throttle - due to some wheelspin he had to manage - and swung from just over a tenth up on Leclerc to 0.25s behind.

Turn 12 was his other big loss, around 0.2s again. Despite again braking earlier, Verstappen did not have the response he needed when he initially started applying steering lock into the corner and ran a little deep, dropping his minimum speed 10km/h below Leclerc's and Antonelli's.

It's possible the Red Bull is not quite as compliant on the bumps in the braking zones here, which is contributing to Verstappen braking slightly earlier and not being as attacking or as confident on entry, or as steady on exit.

"Finding the right balance was more difficult than expected," Wache admitted.

Where Mercedes and McLaren fit in

Antonelli's Mercedes had a more balanced performance profile: quicker on the straights than the Ferrari but not at Red Bull level, but showing good speed on the approach to the hairpin. Potentially, that reflected differences in deployment.

He was strong in Turns 8-9, Turn 15 and Turn 12, but did lose out in several corners on the exits.

McLaren's single-lap pace also looked nowhere on the timesheets, with Lando Norris the faster of its drivers in FP2 but 1.082s off the pace. However, this time was set on hards as he had to abort both of his qualifying simulation laps.

Theoretical best single lap pace FP2

best sector one; best sector two; best sector three | theoretical best

: 25.630s; 37.834s; 31.827s | : 25.754s; 37.460s; 32.119s | : 25.571s; 37.931s; 31.936s | : 25.616s; 37.934s; 32.107s | : 25.662s; 38.092s; 31.998s | : 25.586s; 37.793s; 32.449s | : 25.667s; 37.997s; 32.321s | : 25.620s; 38.098s; 32.311s |

The first was because of a snap mid-corner at Turn 9, possibly the result of running in turbulent air caused by George Russell's Mercedes ahead. His second lap, on soft Pirellis now past their best, was abandoned after a lockup at Turn 15.

"We set a purple [fastest sector time] in FP2 as well, we just didn't finish the lap," said McLaren chief technical officer Rob Marshall. "It was a competitive lap up until the point where we made a mistake.

"Going forward from here we've got to be quite optimistic really."

That first sector time was the fastest at the time he set it, and although it was eclipsed by Verstappen that was only by 0.015s - and it was faster than anything achieved by Ferrari or Mercedes.

On the raw numbers, Norris's McLaren was fastest on the long-run averages in FP2, but it's a confusing picture for a number of reasons.

Traffic affected a number of drivers' long runs and all three tyre compounds were used, so it's tricky to compare a nine-lap Norris run on durable hards to Verstappen's 11-lap soft-tyre run, for example.

But Norris's strong long run backs up McLaren looking stronger than the FP2 result suggested.

Pirelli expects the hard tyre to "play only a limited role in defining race strategies", with a one-stop using the softs and mediums most likely.

Verstappen's soft tyres held up impressively well with consistent laptimes and less of a drop-off compared to Leclerc's.

Team-mate Isack Hadjar was clearly not as comfortable. He struggled with overheating front tyres all day; "it's just a disaster" he said of his soft tyre lap.

"It was just undriveable, and I was losing the front end massively. We need to have a look because that's not normal, why there is so much deg on one lap."

Hadjar said his tyres were "completely killed" in the high-speed corners. Red Bull's Wache said this was key to the difference as he said Hadjar and Verstappen weren't far apart on set-up.

Lewis Hamilton, George Russell, Oscar Piastri and Hadjar all appear to have started the weekend a step behind their respective team-mates.

Hamilton said he "tried a different direction with the set-up, but I wasn't comfortable in the car, especially over the bumps", while Piastri's long run pace on the softs appeared to sharply tail off.

That picture may alter as teams learn overnight lessons and change set-up and deployment patterns, but right now all four teams look like they are in the hunt at Austin.

items.title: What was behind one F1 team's strangest day of 2026
items.author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
items.content:
Williams had a peculiar Friday at the United States Grand Prix as it ended practice with its fastest Formula 1 car slower than Cadillac and the other 8.1 seconds off the pace.

Alex Albon was an exaggerated slowest in FP2 (just as he was in FP1) but the team's real pace was still disappointing, with Carlos Sainz even behind Valtteri Bottas's Cadillac.

A track-limits deletion was behind Albon's particularly unusual deficit and the strangest Friday of 2026 was partly down to Williams sacrificing typical in-weekend work for 2027 development help in FP1.

This meant aero testing on hards in FP1 followed by a short medium-tyre run, as Williams chief trackside engineer Paul Williams said the team had "balanced off performance for this weekend versus long-term learning" because "this track's very good for aero data collection".

Sainz said: "We decided to invest FP1 on a track that we knew we were going to be weak [on] to understand how to basically map the car in order to learn from this year's car as much as possible for next year's car.

"We know we have a lot of weaknesses on this year's car on a track like this and we want to make sure we understand it and we map it to try and get it right next year in the windtunnel."

Then the focus in FP2 was a more standard Friday plan just with a heavier emphasis on high-fuel running as Williams knows its one-lap pace is likely to be lacking anyway - although its long-run pace looked weak in the midfield too.

The Circuit of the Americas is a punishing track as its layout comprises a mix of medium- and high-speed sweeps, long-duration corners, and bumpy heavy braking zones.

This exposes a lot of Williams's underlying weaknesses of recent years and the specific shortcomings of its 2026 car.

In FP2, shortly after Sainz complained the car was a mess and he had no confidence in the rear, Albon reported zero confidence under braking.

"When you have no downforce you're going to suffer either on braking or on high speed," said Sainz.

"We know this year we lack a lot of downforce in the car and especially when it gets bumpy, when it gets high speed, when it gets hot, when it gets windy - like it gets in COTA - the only thing that saves you is downforce and that's what we don't have on this year's car.

"So we're working on it, we are braced for a tough weekend, don't expect any miracles, but at least we are investing in learning as much as possible for next year."

items.title: Winners and losers from COTA's Friday F1 action
items.author: Ben Anderson
items.content:
After a triple-header of races, which culminated in a condensed sprint weekend - followed by a weekend off, Formula 1 teams should be delighted to be back to a typical three-practice weekend.

Only, most of them aren't, because the difficult of setting ride-height correctly on this bumpy circuit on a weekend of so many upgrades and car tweaks has made for a lot of grumpy people in the paddock.

Here's our winners and losers from the practice day.

Loser: Lando Norris (7th)

Sounds as though there might be a bit of a disconnect here between how McLaren feels its Austin Friday went and how its world champion driver feels its Austin Friday went.

Lando Norris was properly quick in FP1, within 0.25s of the pace, and in the FP2 long runs looked reasonable, but the qualifying simulations were a disaster - so much so that he actually went slower (by just under a tenth) in FP2 than he managed in FP1.

The major caveat is that big lock-up Norris had at Turn 15, which came shortly after he’d set the best second sector time of all.

But this is at the crux of it all really. There’s no doubt the McLaren can be a fast car, Norris just maintains it’s “very difficult to drive” and too much on a knife’s edge to be able to readily access that level of performance.

“Like it has been for a long time, it's just too difficult to be able to be consistent, to get a nice feeling consistently,” he added. “The pace is not bad, it's just very difficult to achieve it.

“To get the car to be quick, we just have to try so hard to be perfect, and you cannot be perfect. I'm sure everyone has similar problems in a way, but we're just not quick enough yet, easily, to be there consistently.”

Winner: McLaren (7th & 8th)

What on earth is McLaren doing in our winners' section when Norris was so downbeat and both cars ended FP2 behind a Racing Bulls, you ask?

That's down to the mood higher up at McLaren, which seems a whole lot brighter than Norris's outlook.

Chief technical officer Rob Marshall spoke of the "really small parts" that McLaren has brought to Austin offering a "measurable benefit" that also made a noticeable laptime difference.

That measurable benefit has included an aerodynamic gain with its brake changes, including flow conditioning around the wheels and wake control.

All that led Marshall to conclude that McLaren is in the fight with its main rivals here.

"Going forward from here we've got to be quite optimistic really," he said.

Winner: Charles Leclerc/Ferrari (1st)

An obvious choice of course, considering he topped both Friday sessions, but Leclerc didn’t just look rapid on the soft tyre in FP2.

It looked as though that pace came readily to hand, and the fact he was over six tenths clear of Ferrari team-mate Lewis Hamilton - who had two stabs at a qualifying simulation and set roughly the same lap time on each go - suggests it’s Leclerc in particular who’s got things hooked up for Ferrari in the early phase of this weekend.

The big proviso is the long-run pace, where usually Ferrari would feel its inherent strength lies this season. Has Leclerc’s rapid one-lap speed come at too much of a compromise for tyre degradation? And of course, the perennial question of whether Ferrari can keep up the pace when the engines get turned up for Saturday’s qualifying showdown.

"I think we started the weekend on the right foot with a good balance and I think that is probably the outstanding thing for this Friday," Leclerc said.

"But I also believe the others will start pushing a bit more their cars as they always do coming [into] quali, and so it's going to be tough because it's been a very clean Friday on my side.

"There's more performance in the car, a little bit more, but the others seems to be gaining more than us from the Friday to the Saturday, and seeing the little gap there is... it's not going to be so easy tomorrow."

Winner: Aston Martin (16th & 17th)

Chief trackside officer Mike Krack spoke on Thursday of a need to "manage your expectations a little bit better" in the wake of Aston Martin's misplaced Singapore GP confidence. Fernando Alonso, meanwhile, was quietly talking up the chances of "nice surprises" at the US GP.

Based on Friday practice, Alonso was right to have some optimism. Inside the theoretical Q2 cutoff in both sessions (and up in the dizzying heights of 12th in FP1), with team-mate Lance Stroll for company both times, the Aston Martin looks like a genuine midfield contender again.

Yes, that's still a sign of how the mighty have fallen for a team that so much is expected of, on a day where Adrian Newey spoke of the disappointment Honda was likely to be feeling over its 2026 F1 engine progress.

But in the context of this painful campaign, this was one of the more painless Fridays.

Loser: Isack Hadjar (9th)

OK, run plans, fuel loads and especially at COTA, lap deletions all play a part, but Isack Hadjar failed to get within a second of his Red Bull team-mate Max Verstappen in either practice and called his car's handling disgusting.

Asked to explain his "disgusting" radio comments after practice, Hadjar said "it's just a disaster".

He explained: "From sector one to the end of the lap, I was slower [on the softs] than on the medium. It was just undrivable and I was losing the front end massively. We need to have a look because that's not normal, why is there so much deg on one lap?"

Asking the journalists certainly won't provide the answer, Isack...

Loser: Williams (20th & 22nd)

After being the first team to blatantly and vocally switch its focus from 2025 to get ready for 2026, to be among the first teams to do that two years in a row is the most almighty of damning indictments for where Williams is at.

It was so sure its car would be terrible at Austin that it ran an unusual strategy of compromising this weekend competitively to try to learn how to fix the issues it's having with its handling.

Even Aston Martin - well over four seconds off the pace at the start of the season - didn't admit a switch of focus to 2027, and basically built a new car, which by some stats could have been on pole for the last two races with a different engine.

Anyway, if ruining this weekend gives Williams a huge insight into its troubles for next year, of course it will be worth it it. Until then, it has to suffer the indignity of very publicly having to admit defeat with a 2026 car it was supposed to have a great headstart with.

Winner: Liam Lawson (6th)

Liam Lawson managed to jump both McLarens in FP2, and while that's unlikely on Sunday and perhaps as much down to what was going on with McLaren, it's still a sign the Racing Bulls is working well.

Lawson says "overall the car is in a good place" and that it's "nice to see it working" given the "new stuff" on the car.

More deg than expected and a likely resurgent Nico Hulkenberg - whose Audi team-mate Gabriel Bortoleto beat the Racing Bulls in FP1 but has a grid penalty on Sunday, while Hulkenberg only got new parts in FP2 and is expecting a driveability fix on Saturday - means Lawson isn't out of the woods yet.

And we've seen on more than one occasion this year a Racing Bulls produce an excellent practice lap which doesn't translate into race performance. But that being said, Friday was a good day for Lawson.

Winner: Cadillac (19th & 21st)

No, this isn't based on Valtteri Bottas's 19th place in FP2 ahead of both Williams. But it is based on the way he characterised the day.

"I think we've got the most done that we've ever done in one Friday," said Bottas, who called this something of a test day - but one that ran smoothly and better than expected.

Cadillac still expects this to be a tough weekend; degradation and tyre heating, as Bottas put it, is "definitely not our strength" and that was apparent on Friday. And Cadillac's productiveness also means "it's going to be a busy evening, because like I said with both cars we've tried a lot of different things". (Team-mate Sergio Perez ran an experimental floor, with 2027 in mind, while Bottas ran different front wings and tried different roll stiffnesses.)

Those experimental ideas (which Colton Herta also ran in FP1) were done "to challenge our thinking on the aero concept of the car", as per chief racing officer Marc Hynes, as well as to validate the correlation between Cadillac's CFD and windtunnel work and what it's seeing in the real world.

Based on this reception, it's been a positive Friday's work.

items.title: Marquez falls on his way to staggering Phillip Island MotoGP pole
items.author: Matt Beer
items.content:
Marc Marquez took pole for MotoGP's Australian Grand Prix by a staggering 1.5 seconds at a wet Phillip Island, despite crashing on his first Q2 lap.

With fresh rain falling as Q2 began, that low-side crash into the Miller corner looked like it might leave Marquez a disastrous 12th on the grid.

But he managed to remount his Ducati, the rain eased again, and with the track to himself for his next lap Marquez jumped to pole.

Rain ace Johann Zarco had been fastest at first and did take provisional pole back from Marquez for a while on the next runs.

Then Marquez utterly blew everyone else away on the last laps of the session though, putting in a 1m34.203s that was an astonishing 1.494s faster than the eventual second-place rider, his brother Alex on the Gresini Ducati.

Zarco kept his LCR Honda on the front row in third.

Marquez's title rival Jorge Martin never looked like he had pole pace in the damp but making it back up to fourth on the grid with his last lap counts as a very good save considering Marquez's pace.

Martin's long-shot championship contender Aprilia team-mate Marco Bezzecchi didn't manage that - he starts only ninth for the weekend's two races.

Home hero Jack Miller was fastest in Q1 and briefly had a provisional front row in Q2 before ending up a still heartwarming fifth for Pramac Yamaha.

Performances varied in the conditions, with Marquez's astonishing pole at one end of the field in stark contrast to how far off the pace tail end pair Fabio Quartararo and Franco Morbidelli were in 19th and 20th on the reduced grid that will lack any factory Hondas following the unwell Luca Marini's withdrawal.

items.title: Works Honda team runs out of riders for Australian GP
items.author: Matt Beer
items.content:
The factory Honda MotoGP team will play no further part in the Australian Grand Prix weekend having effectively run out of riders.

Luca Marini was already representing the team solo at Phillip Island but was unwell on Friday and only completed two slow practice laps.

Honda then announced just before Saturday track action started that Marini would not be able to compete this weekend after being declared unfit by MotoGP medical director Dr Angel Charte.

"For the past week, Luca Marini has been suffering from a viral condition and a high fever for three to four days," said Dr Charte.

"For the last 48 to 72 hours, he has been suffering from muscle weakness caused by the virus, affecting both his upper and lower body.

"During the last examination, conducted on Saturday morning, he presented with the same symptoms and was declared unfit."

Marini's team-mate Joan Mir has been absent since mid-September due to an illness that his medical team were struggling to fully diagnose.

There have been suggestions in the paddock this weekend that Mir might be ready to try to return to MotoGP at next week's Malaysian GP - where Marini will also be assessed again.

Though Honda was also in this situation as recently as the September 2024 Misano event, where both Mir and Marini also pulled out with illnesses, the situation is made more bizarre this time by the lack of stand-in options as its two main test riders are both injured.

Taka Nakagami impressed as Mir's Austrian GP replacement but then broke his collarbone in a crash on his very first lap of the following event in Japan.

Aleix Espargaro got the next call-up - with the Indonesian GP his first MotoGP appearance since injuring his back in a test crash in April - but Espargaro withdrew mid-weekend and has since headed for arm pump surgery.

Former LCR rider Somkiat Chantra - now part of Honda's factory World Superbike squad - was also used as Mir's stand-in for Motegi, where Nakagami's aborted entry was as an already-planned wildcard - but Honda has indicated it is keeping him focused on Superbike testing this week.

items.title: What happened in F1 2026 US GP second practice
items.author: Ben Anderson
items.content:
Charles Leclerc kept Ferrari on top in second practice for Formula 1's 2026 United States Grand Prix, narrowly beating Kimi Antonelli's Mercedes and Max Verstappen's Red Bull to the fastest time.

Leclerc topped FP1 around Austin's Circuit of the Americas, but only because Verstappen had a quicker lap deleted for track limits, and it was Verstappen who set the pace early on in FP2 on the medium Pirelli tyres, after finally doing a lap below 1m36s that was legal.

George Russell managed a 1m36.0s for Mercedes early on in FP2, while the Ferraris and Lando Norris's McLaren ran the hard compound tyre and Antonelli spent time in the garage fixing a loose seat that he described as "moving like crazy".

When F1's likely 2026 champion did finally take to the track in anger, out of sequence with the rest, he was two tenths off his Mercedes team-mate.

Leclerc's hard-tyre running was compromised by traffic in the high-speed Esses and getting forced off the circuit by Russell (who was shown a warning flag for his trouble), but on the soft-tyre qualifying simulations the Ferrari came alive and Leclerc went fastest with a 1m35.291s lap.

Antonelli was less than half a tenth away in the best of the Mercedes, while Verstappen lapped just under two tenths off Leclerc, although the later long runs tended to favour Red Bull and Mercedes over the Ferrari in terms of laptime averages.

Behind the top three was a big gap to Lewis Hamilton in the other Ferrari, who completed two very similar flying laps during his qualifying simulation that were both more than six tenths off the pace.

Russell had a huge moment through the Esses on his qualifying run and ended up only fifth, while Liam Lawson capitalised on tricky sessions for both McLarens and the second Red Bull of Isack Hadjar to put Racing Bulls in the top six, all of them more than a second off the pace.

Hadjar sounded very unhappy with his car's balance, while Oscar Piastri had two stabs at a qualifying simulation run and yet still ended up 0.014s off Norris - who went off at Turn 15 on his qualifying run after a huge front axle lockup and so failed to improve upon his earlier hard-tyre laptime.

Ollie Bearman rounded out the top 10 for Haas, just over a tenth down on Hadjar but three tenths clear of Gabriel Bortoleto's Audi, which was top-six fast in the early stages on the harder tyre compounds but gave away relative pace on the soft.

The Aston Martin at this stage looks like a marginal Q2 car, with Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll separated by less than half a tenth of a second, while the Williams looks like the worst car on the track to drive, robbing its drivers of confidence with its unpredictable behaviour and lack of grip.

Alex Albon had a huge moment through the Esses and was slowest of all after failing to set a representative laptime in FP2, as was the case in FP1, while Carlos Sainz was wedged between the Cadillacs in 20th place on the timing sheet, saying "the car is a mess right now".
